etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English wid, wyd, from Old English wīd (“wide, vast, broad, long; distant, far”), from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weydʰh₁- (“to separate, divide”), a dissimilated univerbation from *dwi- (“apart, asunder, in two”) +‎ *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place”).

Cognate with Scots wyd, wid (“of great extent; vast”), West Frisian wiid (“broad; wide”), Dutch wijd (“wide; large; broad”), German weit (“far; wide; broad”), Danish vid (“wide”), Swedish vid (“wide”), Icelandic víður (“wide”), Latin dīvidō (“separate, sunder”), Latin vītō (“avoid, shun”). Related to widow.

definitions.definition: Having a large physical extent from side to side.

quote.citation: 1993, Jacqueline Mitton, The Penguin Dictionary of Astronomy, 2nd edition (paperback), Penguin Books, →ISBN, page 127:
quote.text: Over a wider region either side of the path of totality, a partial eclipse is seen.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Fenella Saunders, “Tiny Lenses See the Big Picture”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: The single-imaging optic of the mammalian eye offers some distinct visual advantages. Such lenses can take in photons from a wide range of angles, increasing light sensitivity. They also have high spatial resolution, resolving incoming images in minute detail.

quote.citation: 2014, Jessica R. Pliley, Policing Sexuality, page 192:
quote.text: Three-way girls offered the widest array of services. One twenty-two-year-old prostitute declared to an undercover vice investigator in New York City, "I am a three-way girl."

definitions.definition: (sports) Operating at the side of the playing area.
On one side or the other of the mark; too far sideways from the mark, the wicket, the batsman, etc.

quote.citation: 1596 (date written; published 1633), Edmund Spenser, A Vewe of the Present State of Irelande […], Dublin:  […]  Societie of Stationers, […], →OCLC; republished as A View of the State of Ireland […] (Ancient Irish Histories), Dublin:  […]  Society of Stationers,  […]  Hibernia Press,  […]  [b]y John Morrison, 1809, →OCLC:
quote.text: Surely he shoots wide on the Bow-Hand.

quote.citation: 1656, Thomas Middleton, William Rowley, Philip Massinger, The Old Law:
quote.text: I was but two bows wide.

definitions.definition: (phonetics, dated) Made, as a vowel, with a less tense, and more open and relaxed, condition of the organs in the mouth.
(Scotland, Northern England, now rare) Vast, great in extent, extensive.
(obsolete) Located some distance away; distant, far. [15th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1748, [Samuel Richardson], “Letter LXXXI”, in Clarissa. Or, The History of a Young Lady: […], volume (please specify |volume=I to VII), London:  […]  S[amuel] Richardson;  […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Mr Hunt's house, you know, lies wide from Harlowe-place.

quote.citation: 1654, H[enry] Hammond, Of Fundamentals in a Notion Referring to Practise, London:  […]  J[ames] Flesher for Richard Royston, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: the contrary [being] so wide from the truth of Scripture and the attributes of God

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Far from truth, propriety, necessity, etc.

quote.citation: 1644, J[ohn] M[ilton], The Doctrine or Discipline of Divorce: […], 2nd edition, London: [s.n.], →OCLC, book:
quote.text: And I trust anon by the help of an infallible guide, to perfect such Prutenic tables, as shall mend the astronomy of our wide expositors.

quote.citation: 1549 April 22 (Gregorian calendar), Hughe Latymer [i.e., Hugh Latimer], Augustine Bernher, compiler, “[27 Sermons Preached by the Ryght Reuerende Father in God and Constant Matir of Iesus Christe, Maister Hugh Latimer, […].] The Syxte Sermon of Maister Hugh Latymer, whiche He Preached before K. Edward [VI], the XII. Day of Aprill.”, in Certayn Godly Sermons, Made uppon the Lords Prayer, […], London:  […]  John Day, […], published 1562, →OCLC, folio 75, verso:
quote.text: But I tell you, it is farre wyde, that the people haue ſuche iudgmentes, the Byſhoppes they coulde laughe at it.

quote.citation: [1633], George Herbert, edited by [Nicholas Ferrar], The Temple. Sacred Poems, and Private Ejaculations, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire:  […]  Thomas Buck and Roger Daniel; and are to be sold by Francis Green, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: How wide is all this long pretence!

definitions.definition: (computing) Of or supporting a greater range of text characters than can fit into the traditional 8-bit representation.

quote.citation: 1951, Josephine Tey, The Daughter of Time, page 31:
quote.text: But the first visitor to penetrate from the outside world proved to be Sergeant Williams; large and pink and scrubbed-looking; and for a little while Grant forgot about battles long ago and considered wide boys alive today.

definitions.definition: away from or to one side of a given goal

quote.citation: 2010 December 29, Sam Sheringham, “Liverpool 0 - 1 Wolverhampton”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: The Reds carved the first opening of the second period as Glen Johnson's pull-back found David Ngog but the Frenchman hooked wide from six yards.

definitions.definition: So as to leave or have a great space between the sides; so as to form a large opening.

quote.citation: 1594, William Shakespeare, Lucrece (First Quarto), London:  […]  Richard Field, for Iohn Harrison, […], →OCLC, line 359:
quote.text: And with his knee the dore he opens wide

definitions.definition: (cricket) A ball that passes so far from the batsman that the umpire deems it unplayable; the arm signal used by an umpire to signal a wide; the extra run added to the batting side's score
